scenes.title: The Wall's Fate
scenes.summary: While Patroclus tends Eurypylus, the poet looks ahead. The wall was built without hecatombs to the gods, and so it will not last: when Hector is dead and Troy sacked and the Argives gone home, Poseidon and Apollo will turn against it all the rivers that run from Ida to the sea, Rhesus, Heptaporus, Caresus, Rhodius, Granicus, Aesepus, Scamander and Simoeis, where the race of half-divine men fell. For nine days Apollo sends their streams against it and Zeus rains, and Poseidon with his trident washes the foundations into the sea and covers the beach with sand again.

scenes.title: Hector at the Ditch
scenes.summary: Now battle blazes around the wall, and the Argives, beaten down by the lash of Zeus, are penned in by the ships in fear of Hector. He ranges like a boar or lion turning on hunters and hounds, whose courage is its death, and urges his companions across the ditch; but the horses balk at the edge, for the ditch is wide, its banks overhang, and it is set with sharp stakes.

scenes.title: Polydamas' Counsel
scenes.summary: Polydamas warns that horsemen cannot fight in the narrow space beyond the stakes, and that if the Achaeans turn and drive them back into the ditch, not even a messenger will get back to the city. Hector agrees and leaps down, and the Trojans leave their chariots with the charioteers and form five columns on foot: Hector, Polydamas and Cebriones; Paris, Alcathous and Agenor; Helenus, Deiphobus and Asius; Aeneas with the two sons of Antenor; and Sarpedon with Glaucus and Asteropaeus at the head of the allies.

scenes.title: Asius at the Gate
scenes.summary: Alone of the Trojans Asius will not leave his horses, and drives for the left of the ships, where the gate stands open for men fleeing from the plain. The poet says that he will never go home, for Idomeneus' spear is waiting for him. At the gate stand the Lapiths Polypoetes and Leonteus, like oaks rooted in the mountains, and when the Trojans rush the wall they come out and fight like wild boars, while stones fall from the towers like snow. Asius groans, strikes his thighs and calls Zeus a lover of lies; but Zeus means to give the glory to Hector.

scenes.title: The Lapiths' Victims
scenes.summary: Fighting goes on at the other gates, and the poet says it is hard for him to tell it all like a god; the gods who help the Danaans grieve. Polypoetes kills Damasus with a spear through the helmet, then Pylon and Ormenus; Leonteus spears Hippomachus, son of Antimachus, then kills Antiphates with his sword, and Menon, Iamenus and Orestes.

scenes.title: The Eagle and the Serpent
scenes.summary: As Hector's men hesitate at the ditch, an eagle flying on the left carries a blood-red serpent in its talons; the serpent bites it at the neck, and the eagle drops it among the Trojans and flies off screaming. Polydamas reads the sign: like the eagle, which never brought its prey home to its young, the Trojans will break the wall but will not come back in good order. Hector, looking darkly at him, says that the gods have taken his wits, that he trusts the counsels of Zeus and cares nothing for birds, and that one omen is best, to fight for one's country; any man who holds back he will kill himself.

scenes.title: The Assault on the Wall
scenes.summary: Zeus raises a wind from Ida that carries the dust against the ships and bewitches the Achaeans. The Trojans tear at the copings and battlements and lever out the buttresses, while the Danaans fence the battlements with oxhides and shoot from behind them. The two Ajaxes range along the towers, rousing the men with gentle words and harsh: there is work now for the best and the worst. The stones fly from both sides as thick as snowflakes on a windless winter day, when Zeus covers mountains and fields and everything but the waves.

scenes.title: Sarpedon and Glaucus
scenes.summary: Zeus rouses his son Sarpedon like a hungry mountain lion that goes after sheep in a guarded fold. Holding his bronze shield before him, Sarpedon tells Glaucus why the two of them are honored in Lycia with the best seats, meat and wine, and a great domain by the Xanthus: they must fight in front, so that the Lycians can say their kings deserve it. If they could escape war and live forever, he would not fight; since death is all around them in any case, they must go and win glory or give it to another.

scenes.title: Menestheus Sends for Ajax
scenes.summary: Menestheus sees the Lycians coming at his tower and, unable to make himself heard over the din, sends the herald Thootes to call the two Ajaxes, or at least Telamonian Ajax and Teucer the archer. Ajax leaves the son of Oileus and Lycomedes to hold their place and goes with Teucer and Pandion, who carries Teucer's bow; they reach the tower as the Lycian leaders are climbing onto the battlements like a dark storm.

scenes.title: The Fight for the Battlement
scenes.summary: Ajax kills Sarpedon's companion Epicles with a jagged boulder that no man of today, even in his prime, could easily hold in both hands, and he falls from the tower like a diver. Teucer wounds Glaucus in the arm, and he slips away unseen. Sarpedon kills Alcmaon, son of Thestor, then seizes a battlement and pulls it down, opening a way into the wall. Teucer's arrow hits his shield strap and Ajax's spear his shield, but Zeus keeps death from his son, and Sarpedon calls on the Lycians to follow. Neither side can drive the other back: they contend like two men disputing a boundary in a common field, and the battle hangs level like the scales of an honest working woman weighing wool for a meager wage.

scenes.title: Hector Breaks the Gate
scenes.summary: Zeus gives Hector the higher glory. He calls on the Trojans to break the wall and throw fire on the ships, picks up a stone that two of the best men of today could not lever onto a wagon, made light for him by Zeus, carries it like a shepherd carrying a fleece, and hurls it at the double doors. The hinges break, the bars give way, and Hector leaps in, his face like swift night, his eyes blazing; no one but a god could stop him. The Trojans pour over the wall and through the gates, and the Danaans flee among the ships.

days.label: Day 26
days.note: The third day of battle continues (11.1 to 18.242). Book 12 follows the fighting at the wall from Polydamas' first counsel to the moment Hector breaks the gate. Patroclus is still in Eurypylus' hut (12.1–2); Book 15 returns to him there as the Trojans storm the wall (15.390–404).
